summary: Lebanon lies on the eastern shore of the Mediterranean, with a diversity of religions and ethnic groups within its borders; it was once called the "Paris of the Middle East", and its political system distributes power along religious sects.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: After the Arab conquest in the 7th century, Sunni Islam became the majority in coastal commercial cities such as Tripoli, Beirut and Sidon, and in the Ottoman period Sunni elites held prominent positions in administration and commerce. Under the 1943 National Pact the prime minister is a Sunni; after the assassination of former prime minister Hariri in 2005, Sunni political forces became even more closely linked with Saudi Arabia.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: Lebanese Christians are mainly of the Maronite Catholic Church, which formed in the 5th century; the Maronites preserved their faith in the northern mountains and united with the Roman Church during the Crusades in the 12th century. There are also Greek Orthodox, Greek Catholic and Armenian churches and others. At the only census, in 1932, Christians slightly outnumbered Muslims, so under the National Pact the president is a Maronite; but since then, because of emigration and a lower birth rate, the Christian share has declined, and the government has never held another census.

ranking.name: Islam (Shia)
ranking.description: Shia Islam has a history of a thousand years in southern Lebanon and the Beqaa Valley, and in the 16th century local Shia scholars were even invited by Iran's Safavid dynasty to go and promote Shia Islam there. For a long time the Shias were mostly poor peasants; from the 1970s the movement led by Musa al-Sadr and, after 1982, the founding of Hezbollah greatly raised the Shias' political standing, and because of a higher birth rate their share continues to rise.

ranking.name: Druze
ranking.description: The Druze faith is a mystical faith that split off in the 11th century from the Ismaili branch in Egypt and took root in the Chouf mountains of Lebanon. In the 17th century the Druze emir Fakhr al-Din II ruled most of Lebanon for a time and is regarded as a forerunner of modern Lebanon; after the clash between the Druze and the Maronites in 1860 their power waned, and today the Jumblatt family is the main political leader.

religion.background: The mountains of Lebanon have been a refuge for religious minorities since ancient times. Christianity had already reached the coastal cities in the 1st century, and from the 5th century the Maronites, named after Saint Maron, formed in the mountains, keeping their Christian faith after the Islamic conquest in the 7th century. In the 11th century the Druze faith took root in the mountains of southern Lebanon. In the Ottoman period, large-scale conflict broke out between the Maronites and the Druze in 1860, European powers intervened, and Mount Lebanon gained autonomy. At independence in 1943, the sects distributed political posts under the National Pact according to population: the president a Maronite, the prime minister a Sunni and the speaker a Shia. This sectarian power-sharing system continues to this day, and the civil war of 1975–1990 was also related to the imbalance in sectarian populations.

language.official: Arabic is the official language, and French also has a special legal status.

ranking.name: Arabic (Lebanese dialect)
ranking.description: Arabic gradually replaced Aramaic after the Islamic conquest in the 7th century, and the Lebanese dialect belongs to Levantine Arabic, retaining quite a few Aramaic words. The constitution makes Arabic the official language; in the 19th century Beirut's newspapers and publishing industry were a center of the Arab Renaissance (Nahda) movement, making an important contribution to the development of Modern Standard Arabic.

ranking.name: Armenian
ranking.description: After the Ottoman Empire's genocide of the Armenians in 1915, large numbers of survivors fled to Lebanon under the French Mandate, and in the 1920s they were settled in places such as Bourj Hammoud in Beirut and gained citizenship. The Armenians kept their own schools, churches and newspapers, so Armenian has continued in Lebanon to this day, with guaranteed seats in parliament.

language.history: The Lebanon region was the homeland of the Phoenicians in antiquity, and the alphabet the Phoenicians invented is the ancestor of the Greek and Latin alphabets. Aramaic later became the common language, and Christian Syriac (a dialect of Aramaic) is still the liturgical language of the Maronite Church. After the Arab conquest in the 7th century Arabic gradually became widespread, and by around the 17th century the Christians of the mountains had also switched to speaking Arabic. The French Mandate of 1920–1943 made French the language of education and the elite; today Lebanese commonly speak Arabic, French and English, often mixing the three in everyday conversation.

ranking.name: Tabbouleh
ranking.description: Mainly plenty of finely chopped parsley, mixed with tomato, mint, onion and a little bulgur (cracked wheat), seasoned with lemon juice and olive oil.
ranking.history: Tabbouleh originates in the mountains of Lebanon and Syria, where in the Middle Ages the inhabitants had the habit of gathering wild herbs to eat, and bulgur is a traditional grain of the Levant. In the 19th to 20th centuries it became widespread in Lebanese cities and became representative of the appetizers (mezze). In 2009 Lebanese chefs made a giant tabbouleh weighing several tonnes to go for a Guinness World Record, which also reflects food-identity disputes such as the "hummus wars" between Lebanon and Israel.

ranking.name: Kibbeh
ranking.description: Crushed wheat is mixed with ground lamb or beef, wrapped around a filling of stir-fried meat and pine nuts, and deep-fried; there is also a raw version (kibbeh nayyeh).
ranking.history: Kibbeh has a history of several hundred years in the Levant and is regarded as one of Lebanon's national dishes. Traditionally women pounded the meat and wheat into a fine meat paste with a stone mortar and wooden pestle, and the sound of pounding meat was once an everyday sound of Lebanese mountain villages. Different regions have different versions: Zgharta in the north is famous for raw kibbeh, and during fasting periods Christians also make meatless kibbeh with pumpkin or potato in place of the meat.

ranking.name: Hummus
ranking.description: A smooth puree of chickpeas, tahini, lemon juice and garlic, drizzled with olive oil and eaten by dipping Arabic flatbread. It often appears together with other appetizers on Lebanese mezze platters.
ranking.history: Chickpeas have been grown in the Levant for thousands of years, and the earliest clear mention of the puree with tahini is in Arabic recipes of around the 13th century. Lebanon is one of the most representative countries for hummus; in 2008 the Association of Lebanese Industrialists tried to apply to the EU to have hummus listed as a Lebanese geographical-indication product, and competed with Israel for the record of the "world's largest hummus"; this "hummus war" reflects the politics of food and national identity.

ranking.name: Fattoush
ranking.description: A salad in which pieces of toasted or fried flatbread are mixed with lettuce, tomato, cucumber, radish and herbs, seasoned with sumac and pomegranate molasses.
ranking.history: The name fattoush comes from the Arabic fatteh (crumbled bread) and originates in the practice in Lebanese villages of toasting or frying day-old Arabic flatbread and mixing it into a salad to avoid waste. Sumac is a sour spice special to the Levant, used to provide sourness before lemons arrived. It is a classic of the Lebanese mezze platter and is especially common at the fast-breaking meal in Ramadan.

ranking.name: Manakish
ranking.description: A breakfast flatbread in which a round dough is spread with thyme spice mix (za'atar) and olive oil, or topped with cheese or ground meat, and baked.
ranking.history: Manakish originates in the baking traditions of Lebanese villages: in the past women baked bread every morning in the communal oven and would make the leftover dough into small flatbreads, spread with za'atar, for breakfast. Za'atar is made of wild thyme, sumac and sesame, and folk belief holds that it "clears the head", so students often eat it before exams. Today it is Lebanon's most common breakfast, and the street-corner bakeries (furn) begin selling it from early morning.
